b: Welcome back to our second installment! If you’d like to catch up from the first post, please visit HERE.

Like most of us I hit the ground running after I got out of school- we were in NYC at the time, pre internet 1993-94, but I was not making a living at it at all at that stage. I had no agent, no illustration connections and living in an apt on Ave C that was so small you had to inhale and hold it to get into certain important parts of it. I had a part time job working as an artists assistant for Joan Snyder, and played gun for hire in similar form ot other painters int he city. Benefit of being in NYC in that time was that was where it all was then, DC, Marvel, all the book publishers of note… NYC was the center of everything so that meant you could go to these places and see about getting something going. Outside of living in NYC you’d need some real connections and you mailed a lot I guess. I don’t know. I didn’t know what I was doing, I hadn’t been trained to be a graphic designer or illustrator and I had decided I was wholly interested in the gallery scene there. I worked like that for a long while it seemed but really it was just a couple of years. Getting a proper space to work in when we moved to a much larger and cheaper place way out on the edge of Windsor Terrace, Brooklyn, near Prospect Park- which was the effing boonies in the early 90’s let me tell you. But I made work, faxed it to publishers and mailed pitches and started to connect with the NY comics scene there. Community and just doing the work was everything. It’s like you need to start building the magnet to start attracting and putting yourself in front of the people you need to be in front of. It was all gatekeepers and connects and zero social media to run and gather a following without them. Different times entirely. But some things were and are still, important.

These below the three most foundational laws you should abide in starting out, and two of them you should hold close and dear until you die of old age at your desk like the heroes of old. What arew they you say? I’m glad you asked:

My grandmother told me once when I was a kid that should I grow up and find myself married, that I was to make sure to obey this one unbreakable law to guarantee as long a marriage as fate will allow: don’t divorce. That simple. and also real hard and not always possible of course. But the principle applies for this thing too- more bso and I think perhaps totally. It’s the single most important pact for anyone fortunate enough to have had a lifelong career as an illustrator, musician, painter, actor, writer… whatever your creative arena is. We have all of us gotten this far because we didn’t stop, we didn’t quit. It’s simple and a little stupid maybe, but it’s true and deeper as a trial and rallying cry than you might otherwise think.It gets hard, and harder than you think you might even be able to survive. There were MANY months where I came up short on rent, had to get an advance on a job through my manager, and still worked another job as a housepainter/home repairer/sheetrocker, whatever during most of the days and made sure I worked at night after I got home. weekends too. I was broke for most of it, said no to a lot of fun parties and worked. My first graphic novel, SUDDEN GRAVITY was something I had made up and just started doing after I found an indy publisher Caliber Comics, to print it. I worked on that book for years, entirely for free, just to have it see print. nights and weekends and holidays and when I was sick and all the rest. And when the publisher was going down before I had finished the series I had to double down and get the last double sized issue out before that door closed too. I was rejected endlessly, pitching things I thought at the time were genius things… that were most definitely not. But I had printed and published comics to take with me on my very first trip to San Diego Comicon, in hopes of meeting my heroes that inspired me to working in comics, Dave McKean, George Pratt, Jon Muth, Kent Williams, Jeffery Catherine Jones, etc… and their manager Allen Spiegel. That was the target I aimed for and when I rolled up to the booth to make that connection I knew was going to change everything… Allen barely regarded me and I slinked away like a field mouse. I managed to connect with one of his new clients, Jaime Tolagson, and we bonded right away and began corresponding after, but I was sure I had blown it. All that expense and time and didn’t feel like I had much of anything to show for it. I had a book series at Vertigo comics years later that got cancelled mid stream out of the blue because the publisher personally disliked my editor and when he was fired for a production screw up, she killed every book he ran regardless of where it was in the pipeline. I got what looked like a standard rejection letter she’d xeroxed maybe thirty thousand times it was so scumbly… a total kiss off. I’ve had a graphic novel I’ve worked on for three years hit and die when published because of the Covid pandemic, watched favorite publishers go belly up, and my creative partners scatter, and some of my most favorite things just die or land with a thud, and spent a season of the most depressing pitch meetings during the financial crash of ’08 where every publishing house was like a charnel house during the plague times. I was working on a poster for the anniversary of Wong Kar-Wai’s IN THE MOOD FOR LOVE, and it was excellent lush and gorgeous and… he didn’t like it. I tried another and also got rejected, and even when Eric my AD at Mondo called me to say we tried our best, I asked for one more day to try something new, and if that failed we could surrender. I had no idea what that would be and I had 24 hours to figure it out. It turned out to be something so utterly different from what I had been doing as to be the hail-maryest of hail-mary passes… and Wong loved it one of my most iconic film posters to date was born. You just never know what lies at the end of the dark and horrible road, but you certainly won’t ever find out if you quit. These are but a tiny few of the myriad of examples, roadblocks, accidents, financial disasters, personal catastrophes, and just plain old bad luck that I’ve gotten to live through, and any one of them could rightly have chased me from this as a career. I’d like to say it was because I was lucky or rested comfortably on a well seasoned trust fund, or was perhaps just an insane person… but the truth is I just never quit. So here I am.

Be ready for it to look VERY different from what you were expecting, and to lead you to places you never thought you’d go… (I for one never imagine=d in my life I’d be doing movie posters or LP designs, but here I am). Your illustration dream might chase you into being a professor at an art school, or an art director at a publishing house. You really can;t know. Bend like a reed, be smart as you can about exploiting the resources around you, work and then keep working and don’t stop.
IN THE BEGINNING… SAY YES TO EVERYTHING

Sure you have an idea to be this kind of illustrator, to work in that kind of field, or whatever… we all have our areas of interest and expertise, and largely that will be whatever it was that drove us to make a go at this life in the first place. You have that center and should absolutely keep working it properly, polishing and improving, but that doesn’t mean you need to be monogamous to it starting out. In fact I’d suggest you are doing yourself no favors by only chasing the one narrow lane of the industry you want to breach into. Yes you already have a voice, but you’re too green to hear it yet. You have a career goal even as a dream, but you have no idea what the road to that summit will be. Believe me you have NO IDEA. There’s no harm in it. Just say yes. Get an offer to do a political cartoon for a local free paper, YES, do it. a buddy of yours heard of an office that’s looking for someone to draw portraits of their management for a newsletter, grab it and run. It’s all practice and I’ve done them all myself. If they don’t seem to make connections that lead you to where you want to be, you’re probably wrong. I can draw a direct line between working at Dark Horse Comics, getting to know an editor who pushed me hard into drawing a Conan comic for 6 issues which Ethan Hawke found in a shop on Broadway, that led to cowriting and drawing a graphic novel telling a story of the Chiricahua Apaches, a crime story that was rooted in our struggles with our own sons and so many other things including a nearly two-decade long friendship. So you just never know. Do the best you can do at all times because you never know who might be watching.

But you’re a fresh leaf and you want to gather every ray of sunlight to grow from, so collect all the opportunities that you can, and the bad ones will teach you as much or more than the good ones. You’re too new to know what you don’t know or know even the vast sea of potential worlds to swim in, so test them all and see what fiots. You will be surprised by what you end up falling in love with. I know I was.

Bringing your full game to ALL the games, also means you are being your best self at these jobs which makes the work so much better, encourages your radar to be on the lookout for brilliant inspirations that can kick a project ten levels upward. And you can walk away from your workday feeling the blush of pride of simply having had done your best. It sounds corny but it’s a real value… if if your landlord won’t take it in lieu of a check for rent. The work always rewards itself, and every opportunity is one to make yourself better at your job. Be prepared and open to weird paths that can come up, connections you didn’t know you’d make. be friendly and as happy warrior wherever you find your niche, and be prepared for big changes. My career’s had a lot of different focuses and among the half dozen or so over the last thirty years, only one of them was a planned to do item- comics. When your wheels get turning and find yourself getting traction, you can start saying no to approaches from a place of experience and wisdom, and not necessarily needing to say yes to all the things. Sometimes what someone thinks you’ll be awesome for is not awesome to you.

Work as if the job you’re on is the last job you will ever have… because if you don’t it might be. if things go pear shaped, don’t be the one who blew it up. if you have to bail on something, and sometimes you just have to, make sure it’s as soft a landing as possible for your client, even if they are terrible. The secret long term super power you need to understand ties back to the small world of illustration and publishing where everyone knows each other. The assistants and deputy ADs, and young turks just entering that side of publishing are also watching how things go, and if your client is being terrible, but you behave like an adult and handle it well and right, those young turks will grow up int heir careers too, and they will remember how you handled a bad job. I can’t tell you how many times I find myself working for a new publisher on a book job, or a poster thing, or a film package where someone on the team, if not the team’s head were an assistant editor on a job as long as ten or fifteen years back, and have had affirmed that witnessing grace under fire during a bad turn endeared them to working with you later when the could do things differently.
ALWAYS MAKE IT ABOUT THE WORK

We love our work are emotionally connected to it and the passion that engenders is an essential tool for powering through hard and glorious times alike. It’s an amazing feeling when you’re working for a company or with an editor/AD who gets this and knows artists enough to know they have a soft squishy side of them that loves what they do deeply, because it can be a vulnerable place that needs protecting. The process of working as an illustrator- particularly the business office people you will be working with, especially the horrid committees you won’t be able to escape is, is more an act of reducing harm to your core work, getting through the brambles, unquestionably bad ideas and suggestions, and even the good ones that can fundamentally alter your course. in the last 30+ years I can count on one hand how many of those projects sailed through on their own everything arrived at press 100% what I had intended going in with. If I can hit press with 75-80% of the core values of a piece intact, I consider that an incredible victory. It can be a heartbreak factory, but it’s less so if you give yourself some emotional space from that process, be realistic about what you can achieve, and never let the inherent desire to make simple and bland a situation you accept as true. It gives you a clear head to push through and I find a wider field to capture solutions in.

It helps also with your successes too. I’m notoriously weird about giving sports-like trophies to art as a baseline principle, and it helps to keep the work as a separate entity so you don’t become a bit over drunk on your victory. Enjoy it and celebrate your work by all and every means, but know it too, like all the bad times that will come also, will pass. I think there’s nothing more damaging to a new fresh illustrator than having a massive hit and art awards too early. it can poison your growth and create a dynamic where you waste years or your career trying to re-please the audience that loved something early on, catch that lightening again, even though you forgot that you weren’t chasing lightening when you caught it the last time. It makes you a subject of your success not a captain of it. It takes hundreds of hours thousands of drawings to get to your best self as an artist, and that means being un-precious about your work and yourself as you go. There is no plateau or apex point where you can stop and rest on your laurels- the whole point is to never stop climbing, and never reach the top. It’s why we retire by way of the grave, instead of putting down our labors at the end of the long day of our lives to putter around the garden and play golf. THIS is your garden, this is your play. Most people will not understand this, and it’s important to establish a clear and balanced head about your work so you can see it from their perspective as well. Your audience deserves your understanding of them, warts and all. The work is better for it.

Not putting yourself at your career’s center is a gift you will reap the rewards from your whole life. It’s ballast when you need it, helps you make the right choices about your projects and less susceptible to being sold into a job you should not be in. Having even that single breath’s distance doesn’t diminish the personal emotional experience with the work- it in fact enhances and grows it. It provides you with the ability to see it more clearly and appreciate it or spot goofs that you the artist might miss but the outsider sees. It affords you the wisdom to parlay the situation in the best way for the work- because it’s always about the next project, especially when you’ve come to the end of the one you’re on. Some projects despite being offered to you aren’t really for you at all, and being able to hear your own voice say this to you before you sign the contract can save you literal years of suffering and very big public relationship burning disasters. It also opens up your canvas to imperfect clients and imperfect publishers where you can still achieve something great, BECAUSE you have the distance and experience to know how to brushg off the small dumb stuff for the greater goals you can achieve with the project. The sure things aren’t always so sure, and you need to have the perspective to see it. All of this can be supported and grown fully and practically with a lot of help from our last subject in this month’s article…

We’re all of us have a bit of the troglodyte in us. You have to to do this work, comics especially… but all illustration really boils down to hours of time alone in a room with your work while your social cool friends are out have a blast at a bar or a punk show in the Bowery. (yes I’m utterly aware of how dated this last sentence boxes me into). It’s an inherently lonely enterprise and of course important to be okay with spending so much time alone in your head… BUT remember to note that everyone else doing this is also doing this. Some of us are more sociable than others, but all of us need our society to grow in this field. To have colleagues and friends made through the life of an illustrator is one of the medium’s true lasting gifts. Yuko Shimizu once said she was an illustrator because she wanted to reach the wodest possible audience for her work. And that’s a true thing- and makes our small communities even more essential when we’re dancing on such a vast stage.

I love my community so deeply I can’t put into words, even though I am personally, by comparison, much more of a lone wolf type than many of them. But I also know that when the chips are down, they have my back and I theirs. That when there’s a massive issue in the industry, apes are stronger together. They are your resource for how to buy the best scanner for your studio, paint brush for your canvas work, pencil sharpener for your pencils, and as an early warning system for toxic clients, and the great ones. When I get approached by a new client I don’t know, I will reach out to any colleague of mine who have worked with them and mine them for all they can offer in terms of giving me a heads up about their ethics, approach, work style, pay scale and quality of publishing. When I mentioned earlier that this is a small world made even smaller by social media, I meant it. That community can be your armor against a bad situation, and warn you off of otherwise catastrophic relationships, grifts and avoidable crises from bad actors. We all talk with each other and share good news and bad throughout. There is also little in life more fun than sitting around with colleagues sharing war stories. It is bananas what we go through and being able to share and laugh at it later, of discover in that sharing that you had the same experience is a deeply enriching warming thing. So make sure to create and value the village you live and work in, because there’s power in families, refuge and cheerleading in them that you will want and need in your life. No matter how alone we are most of the time by the basic nature of the work, these community moments are what keeps our hearts filled pushing through into the dark.
